# Playbook

**When I'm told the sustainable share, I start there.** It's the rate that keeps the stock flat. In any season except the last, catching the sustainable share guarantees I earn the same amount every remaining season. Deviating upward costs me more in lost future seasons than it gains in the current one, because the stock drop compounds.

**In the final season, I take a dominant share of the remaining stock.** I estimate what each other boat will likely catch based on their full history (their average, their trend, whether they've been conservative or aggressive), subtract that from the stock, and take a large fraction of what's left. In practice this means aiming for 55–70% of the stock, not just "a big number." Being timid in the final round is the single biggest way to leave points on the table, and in my last episode I took 52% when I likely could have taken more given the other boats' predictable patterns.

**I do not overfish in early seasons to "get ahead."** A small overage in season 1 shrank my per-season income for every subsequent season. The compounding loss outweighs the one-time gain. If I want to extract extra value, the final season is where I do it, not scattered across the middle.

**I watch what the other boats actually catch, not what I expect them to catch.** If they are consistently overfishing, the stock will drop regardless of my restraint. In that case I adjust my expectation of the stock trajectory rather than assuming it stays flat, and I lean harder into the final-season grab because the middle seasons will be worth less.

**If the stock is dropping season over season, I do not try to compensate by cutting my own catch below sustainable.** The others' overfishing is already driving the decline; my extra restraint doesn't stop it, it just gives them more. I hold at sustainable (or slightly above if the stock is still healthy) and save my aggression for the last round.

**If the stock is stable and everyone is at sustainable, I stay put through the middle seasons and concentrate all my extra ambition into the final round.** This is the cleanest way to maximize total: reliable income for N−1 seasons plus one big final grab.

**I do not try to outsmart the others into a "tragedy of the commons" standoff in the middle seasons.** If I'm the only one restricting while others overfish, I'm the one losing. The only rational deviation from sustainable is upward, and the only rational time for that is the last season.

**In the final season, I factor in that some other boats will also go aggressive.** A boat that has been overfishing all game is likely to go even harder in the last round. I don't assume everyone stays at their historical average. I estimate the most aggressive plausible catch from each other boat and still take a large share of what remains. If the stock is 66.8 and I estimate the other two boats will take 25 combined, I aim for 38–42, not 35.

**My total score may not equal my total submitted catch.** In my last episode, my submitted catches summed to 84.0 but my final score was 62.9. There may be a penalty, a scaling mechanism, or a relative scoring rule I haven't fully identified. I should not assume "catch as much as possible in the final round" is always optimal if it depletes the stock to near-zero — there may be a penalty for that. I'll keep my final-season grab large but not so large that it wipes the stock out entirely; I'll leave a small buffer.

**Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)**

When a season is not the final one, submit exactly the sustainable share shown for the current stock level. Do not overfish to freeride — the one-time gain is smaller than the compounding loss in future sustainable yield.

When the final season is put to me, submit the entire remaining stock. I will not get all of it if others also fish heavily (allocation appears to be proportional or capped when total submissions exceed the stock), but I will get substantially more than the sustainable share. Going big is still the dominant move.

When the stock level has changed from what it was at the start, recalculate my target from the new sustainable share shown to me, not from my original plan.

When others are clearly overfishing and the stock is declining, I still match the current sustainable share. I do not overfish in retaliation or to "get ahead" of a collapse I cannot prevent unilaterally. Preserving the stock through conservative play in non-final seasons is what keeps a large pool available for my final-season grab.

When I am uncertain whether others will overfish in a non-final season, I err toward the sustainable share. A modest overfishing gamble only pays off if the stock survives, and the downside (reduced yield every remaining season plus a smaller final-season pool) is nearly always larger than the upside.

The final-season grab is the payoff for all the restraint in earlier seasons. The more stock I preserve by matching the sustainable share, the more is available to capture in the last round. This is the core logic: be conservative early, be maximal at the end.

# Playbook

The sustainable share per boat equals stock divided by 9. Use this for quick calculations.

When the game is the last season, do NOT take the full stock. In my last episode, submitting the entire stock (66.8) only yielded an effective ~26.5 toward my score, not the full amount. There is either a cap on single-season catch or a penalty for maximal extraction. Aim for a large but bounded figure — roughly 25–30, or about 40% of the current stock, whichever is smaller. The exact mechanism is unclear, but going maximal clearly backfired and left points on the table.

When the game is not the last season and I am the one taking more than the sustainable share (the other boats are at or near sustainable), maintain a consistent premium. In my episode, taking 14 while the others took the sustainable share (10.5, 9.9, 9.2, 8.3) built a large and comfortable lead (71 vs. 49 after five seasons). A consistent premium is better than a varying one because it is predictable and the stock dynamics become simple.

The key dynamic: if I take a premium of d above the sustainable share in a given season, the stock drops by 1.5 × d at the end of that season (compared to the path where I took sustainable). This means my sustainable share next season falls by d/6. Over the remaining seasons, the cumulative cost of a constant premium d is modest — the net gain of taking a small premium is almost always positive as long as the stock doesn't approach zero.

When the stock is at or near the cap (100), I can afford a larger initial premium because the absolute stock loss (1.5d) is small relative to the total, and the stock has the most room to absorb it. A premium of ~4 (taking 15 vs. sustainable 11.1) was good in season 1.

When I notice another boat taking significantly more than the sustainable share for two or more consecutive seasons, match their take. If the stock is being depleted by others' overfishing, I should not be the one left behind taking a smaller share of a shrinking pie.

Do not anchor on the "sustainable share" number as a moral limit. It is the cooperative equilibrium, not the individual optimum. My score depends only on my total landed, not on the stock's health per se. The stock matters only insofar as it determines what I can take in future seasons.

When in doubt between two options in a non-final season, choose the one that is slightly higher. The cost of overfishing by a small amount is spread across future seasons and is usually less than the immediate gain, especially with fewer than four seasons remaining.

Track the stock trajectory explicitly. If the stock is declining by more than ~8 per season, I am overfishing relative to the remaining horizon and should consider trimming my premium to avoid a collapse that eliminates my last-season catch. A stock below ~40 with more than one season left is dangerous territory.
